title: Das singende springende Löweneckerchen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 88. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 88, whose title is the first puzzle: a Löweneckerchen is no little lion but a lark, a dialect word Grimm glosses inside the text itself as (Lerche). A father asks his three daughters what to bring home from his journey — pearls, diamonds, and, from the youngest, a singing, springing lark — and finds the bird guarded by a lion who will sell it only for whatever first meets the man at his own door. What follows begins as a beast-bridegroom match and then breaks it open: a ray of candlelight no wider than a hair turns the lion-husband into a dove, and his wife walks seven years behind a trail of blood-drops and white feathers, questioning the sun, the moon and the four winds, before buying him back from a rival with a dress of sunlight and a hen with twelve golden chicks. Spelling follows the 1857 edition (daß, muß, gieng, fieng, thun/that, Thür, Rath, Noth, ward).

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Mann, der hatte eine große Reise vor, und beim Abschied fragte er seine drei Töchter was er ihnen mitbringen sollte.
sentences.l: There was once a man, he had a great journey in prospect, and at the leave-taking he asked his three daughters what he should bring them.
sentences.i: There was once a man who had a long journey before him, and as he took his leave he asked his three daughters what he should bring back for them.
sentences.n: Es war einmal is the fixed opening of a German tale, our “once upon a time.” der hatte is the loose relative of the tales — literally “a man, he had” — where English says “who had.” vorhaben is separable, so its particle vor stands off at the end: hatte … vor, “had in prospect, was planning.”

sentences.t: Da wollte die älteste Perlen, die zweite wollte Diamanten, die dritte aber sprach „lieber Vater, ich wünsche mir ein singendes springendes Löweneckerchen (Lerche).“
sentences.l: Then the eldest wanted pearls, the second wanted diamonds, but the third said “dear father, I wish myself a singing springing Löweneckerchen (lark).”
sentences.i: Then the eldest wanted pearls, the second wanted diamonds, but the third said, “Dear father, I should like a singing, springing lark.”
sentences.n: Löweneckerchen is a dialect name for the lark; the round-bracket gloss (Lerche) stands in the 1857 text itself — it is the Grimms’ own, not supplied here. sich etwas wünschen puts the wisher in the dative, literally “I wish myself,” where English says “I should like.”

sentences.t: Der Vater sagte „ja, wenn ich es kriegen kann, sollst du es haben,“ küßte alle drei und zog fort.
sentences.l: The father said “yes, if I can get it, you shall have it,” kissed all three and moved off.
sentences.i: The father said, “Yes, if I can get it, you shall have it,” kissed all three and set out.
sentences.n: kriegen is the everyday word for getting hold of something. fortziehen is separable: zog … fort, “moved off.” In the 1857 printing the comma sits inside the closing quotation mark.

sentences.t: Als nun die Zeit kam, daß er wieder auf dem Heimweg war, so hatte er Perlen und Diamanten für die zwei ältesten gekauft,
sentences.l: When now the time came that he was on the homeward way again, so he had bought pearls and diamonds for the two eldest,
sentences.i: Now when the time came for him to be on his way home again, he had bought pearls and diamonds for the two eldest,
sentences.n: The so that picks up a leading subordinate clause has no English equivalent; “then” or nothing is as close as it comes. daß is the 1857 spelling of dass.

sentences.t: aber das singende springende Löweneckerchen für die jüngste hatte er umsonst aller Orten gesucht, und das that ihm leid, denn sie war sein liebstes Kind.
sentences.l: but the singing springing Löweneckerchen for the youngest he had sought in all places in vain, and that made him sorry, for she was his dearest child.
sentences.i: but the singing, springing lark for the youngest he had hunted for everywhere in vain, and he was sorry for it, for she was his dearest child.
sentences.n: umsonst here means “in vain,” not “for nothing.” aller Orten is an old frozen genitive, “of all places, everywhere.” that is the 1857 past of thun (modern tat, tun), in the set phrase es thut mir leid, “I am sorry.”

sentences.t: Da führte ihn der Weg durch einen Wald, und mitten darin war ein prächtiges Schloß, und nah am Schloß stand ein Baum,
sentences.l: Then the way led him through a wood, and in the middle of it was a splendid castle, and near the castle stood a tree,
sentences.i: Then his road took him through a forest, and in the midst of it stood a splendid castle, and close by the castle stood a tree,
sentences.n: darin is “therein,” pointing back to the wood: mitten darin, “right in the middle of it.” The verb keeps second place, so an opening Da throws the subject der Weg behind führte.

sentences.t: ganz oben auf der Spitze des Baums aber sah er ein Löweneckerchen singen und springen.
sentences.l: but right up on the top of the tree he saw a Löweneckerchen sing and spring.
sentences.i: but right at the top of the tree he saw a lark singing and hopping.
sentences.n: aber stands after the first phrase rather than at the head of the clause, as it constantly does in these tales; it still means “but.” sah … singen und springen is the bare infinitive after a verb of perception, English “saw it sing.”

sentences.t: „Ei, du kommst mir gerade recht“ sagte er ganz vergnügt und rief seinem Diener, er sollte hinauf steigen und das Thierchen fangen.
sentences.l: “Ah, you come to me just right” said he quite delighted and called to his servant, he should climb up and catch the little creature.
sentences.i: “Well, you have come at just the right moment,” he said, quite delighted, and called to his servant to climb up and catch the little creature.
sentences.n: gerade recht kommen is a set phrase, “to come at just the right moment.” rufen takes the dative of the person called to. er sollte … is reported command, where English uses an infinitive, “to climb up.” Thierchen is the 1857 spelling of Tierchen, the diminutive of Thier.

sentences.t: Wie er aber zu dem Baum trat, sprang ein Löwe darunter auf, schüttelte sich und brüllte, daß das Laub an den Bäumen zitterte.
sentences.l: But as he stepped up to the tree, a lion sprang up under it, shook himself and roared, so that the foliage on the trees trembled.
sentences.i: But when he stepped up to the tree, a lion sprang up from underneath it, shook himself and roared until the leaves on the trees trembled.
sentences.n: wie here means “when,” not “how” — one of the commonest turns in the tales. aufspringen is separable: sprang … auf. daß after a description of manner gives the result, “so that.”

sentences.t: „Wer mir mein singendes springendes Löweneckerchen stehlen will,“ rief er, „den fresse ich auf.“
sentences.l: “Whoever wants to steal from me my singing springing Löweneckerchen,” he cried, “him I eat up.”
sentences.i: “Whoever means to steal my singing, springing lark from me,” he cried, “him I shall devour.”
sentences.n: mir is the dative of the person robbed, “steal from me.” The pair Wer … den sets the object den at the head of the second clause, which English cannot copy. fressen is what animals do, essen what people do; auffressen is to devour outright.

sentences.t: Da sagte der Mann „ich habe nicht gewußt, daß der Vogel dir gehört:
sentences.l: Then the man said “I have not known that the bird belongs to you:
sentences.i: Then the man said, “I did not know that the bird was yours:
sentences.n: gehören takes the dative: dir gehört, “belongs to you.” German uses the perfect habe … gewußt where English prefers the plain past, “did not know.” gewußt is the 1857 spelling of gewusst.

sentences.t: ich will mein Unrecht wieder gut machen, und mich mit schwerem Golde loskaufen, laß mir nur das Leben.“
sentences.l: I will make my wrong good again, and buy myself free with heavy gold, only leave me my life.”
sentences.i: I will make my wrong good again and ransom myself with heavy gold — only leave me my life.”
sentences.n: wieder gut machen is the set phrase for making amends. Golde carries the old dative -e, long since dropped. laß mir das Leben has the dative of the person concerned, “leave me my life, spare me.”

sentences.t: Der Löwe sprach „dich kann nichts retten, als wenn du mir zu eigen versprichst, was dir daheim zuerst begegnet;
sentences.l: The lion said “you nothing can save, except if you promise me as my own what first meets you at home;
sentences.i: The lion said, “Nothing can save you unless you promise me as my own whatever first meets you at home;
sentences.n: sprach is the old narrative past of sprechen, “said,” where modern German would use sagte. dich stands first as object, which German may do freely and English cannot. begegnen takes the dative: dir … begegnet, “meets you.”

sentences.t: willst du das aber thun, so schenke ich dir das Leben und den Vogel für deine Tochter obendrein.“
sentences.l: but will you do that, so I grant you your life and the bird for your daughter into the bargain.”
sentences.i: but if you will do it, then I grant you your life and the bird for your daughter into the bargain.”
sentences.n: A German condition can be built by putting the verb first: willst du das aber thun means “but if you will do that.” thun is the 1857 spelling of tun. schenken is to give as a gift, here of sparing a life.

sentences.t: Der Mann aber weigerte sich und sprach „das könnte meine jüngste Tochter sein, die hat mich am liebsten und läuft mir immer entgegen, wenn ich nach Haus komme.“
sentences.l: But the man refused and said “that could be my youngest daughter, she has me dearest and always runs toward me when I come home.”
sentences.i: But the man refused, and said, “That could be my youngest daughter; she loves me best and always comes running to meet me when I come home.”
sentences.n: jemanden am liebsten haben is “to love someone best,” literally to have someone most dearly. entgegenlaufen is separable and takes the dative: läuft mir … entgegen, “runs to meet me.”

sentences.t: Dem Diener aber war angst und er sagte „muß euch denn gerade eure Tochter begegnen, es könnte ja auch eine Katze oder ein Hund sein.“
sentences.l: But to the servant it was fearful and he said “must your daughter of all things meet you, it could just as well be a cat or a dog.”
sentences.i: But the servant was frightened, and said, “Must it be your daughter that meets you? It could just as well be a cat or a dog.”
sentences.n: mir ist angst is impersonal: the person stands in the dative and there is no subject at all — “to the servant it was fearful” — where English gives him the subject and says he was frightened. euch and eure are the polite plural: the servant addresses his master as ihr, which comes into English simply as “you, your.”

sentences.t: Da ließ sich der Mann überreden, nahm das singende springende Löweneckerchen und versprach dem Löwen zu eigen was ihm daheim zuerst begegnen würde.
sentences.l: Then the man let himself be persuaded, took the singing springing Löweneckerchen and promised the lion as his own what should first meet him at home.
sentences.i: Then the man let himself be talked round, took the singing, springing lark, and promised the lion as his own whatever should first meet him when he came home.
sentences.n: sich überreden lassen — lassen with an infinitive is German’s way of saying “to let oneself be persuaded.” würde is the subjunctive of reported speech, the promise as the man himself would have put it.

sentences.t: Wie er daheim anlangte und in sein Haus eintrat, war das erste, was ihm begegnete, niemand anders als seine jüngste liebste Tochter:
sentences.l: When he arrived home and stepped into his house, the first that met him was none other than his youngest, dearest daughter:
sentences.i: When he got home and walked into his house, the first thing to meet him was none other than his youngest and dearest daughter:
sentences.n: anlangen is the older word for arriving. begegnen takes the dative: ihm begegnete, “met him.” The colon hangs the next clause on this one, where English would want a dash or a fresh sentence.

sentences.t: die kam gelaufen, küßte und herzte ihn, und als sie sah, daß er ein singendes springendes Löweneckerchen mitgebracht hatte, war sie außer sich vor Freude.
sentences.l: she came running, kissed and hugged him, and when she saw that he had brought a singing springing Löweneckerchen with him, she was beside herself for joy.
sentences.i: she came running, kissed and hugged him, and when she saw that he had brought a singing, springing lark, she was beside herself with joy.
sentences.n: kam gelaufen pairs a verb of motion with a participle, exactly as English does in “came running.” mitbringen is separable: mitgebracht hatte. außer sich vor Freude is the set phrase, beside oneself with joy.

sentences.t: Der Vater aber konnte sich nicht freuen, sondern fieng an zu weinen und sagte „mein liebstes Kind, den kleinen Vogel habe ich theuer gekauft,
sentences.l: But the father could not rejoice, but began to weep and said “my dearest child, the little bird I have bought dear,
sentences.i: But the father could take no joy in it; instead he began to weep, and said, “My dearest child, I have paid dearly for the little bird,
sentences.n: sich freuen is reflexive, literally to gladden oneself. fieng an is the 1857 spelling of fing an, from the separable anfangen. theuer (modern teuer) means dear in price as well as dear in affection, and the tale is using both at once.

sentences.t: ich habe dich dafür einem wilden Löwen versprechen müssen, und wenn er dich hat, wird er dich zerreißen und fressen,“
sentences.l: I have had to promise you for it to a wild lion, and when he has you, he will tear you apart and devour you,”
sentences.i: I have had to promise you for it to a wild lion, and once he has you he will tear you to pieces and eat you,”
sentences.n: versprechen müssen is the double infinitive: a modal in the perfect appears as an infinitive, not a participle. dafür, “for that,” points back to the bird. The tale does not soften what the lion will do, and the English does not either.

sentences.t: und erzählte ihr da alles, wie es zugegangen war, und bat sie nicht hin zu gehen, es möchte auch kommen was da wollte.
sentences.l: and told her then everything, how it had come about, and begged her not to go there, let come what would.
sentences.i: and then he told her the whole of it, how it had come about, and begged her not to go, come what might.
sentences.n: zugehen is used of things happening: wie es zugegangen war, “how it had come about.” es möchte auch kommen was da wollte is the old formula of resignation; both verbs stand in the subjunctive, so it is a wish let go of rather than a statement.

sentences.t: Sie tröstete ihn aber und sprach „liebster Vater, was ihr versprochen habt muß auch gehalten werden:
sentences.l: But she comforted him and said “dearest father, what you have promised must also be kept:
sentences.i: But she comforted him and said, “Dearest father, what you have promised must be kept:
sentences.n: ihr is the polite plural the children use to their father; it comes into English simply as “you.” The passive gehalten werden keeps the promise as subject, as English does too.

sentences.t: ich will hingehen und will den Löwen schon besänftigen, daß ich wieder gesund zu euch komme.“
sentences.l: I will go there and will surely soothe the lion, so that I come back to you sound.”
sentences.i: I will go, and I shall soften the lion, never fear, so that I come back to you safe and sound.”
sentences.n: schon here is not “already” but the confident particle, “never fear.” hingehen is separable, the hin marking motion away toward the place. gesund is “in health,” here safe and sound.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen ließ sie sich den Weg zeigen, nahm Abschied und gieng getrost in den Wald hinein.
sentences.l: The next morning she had the way shown to her, took leave and went confidently into the wood.
sentences.i: Next morning she had the road pointed out to her, took her leave, and went into the forest with a good heart.
sentences.n: sich etwas zeigen lassen — lassen with an infinitive is “to have something done.” gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging. getrost is of good courage, unafraid.

sentences.t: Der Löwe aber war ein verzauberter Königssohn, und war bei Tag ein Löwe, und mit ihm wurden alle seine Leute Löwen,
sentences.l: But the lion was an enchanted king’s-son, and was by day a lion, and with him all his people became lions,
sentences.i: But the lion was an enchanted prince, and by day he was a lion, and with him all his people became lions,
sentences.n: Königssohn is a glued compound, king’s son, hyphenated in the literal to show the join; it is the tales’ ordinary word for a prince.

sentences.t: in der Nacht aber hatten sie ihre natürliche menschliche Gestalt.
sentences.l: in the night, however, they had their natural human shape.
sentences.i: but at night they had their own natural human form.
sentences.n: Gestalt is shape or form, the word the tales use for the outward body a person is wearing at the moment.

sentences.t: Bei ihrer Ankunft ward sie freundlich empfangen und in das Schloß geführt.
sentences.l: At her arrival she was kindly received and led into the castle.
sentences.i: On her arrival she was kindly received and led into the castle.
sentences.n: ward is the old passive auxiliary, modern wurde; it runs through the whole book.

sentences.t: Als die Nacht kam, war er ein schöner Mann und die Hochzeit ward mit Pracht gefeiert.
sentences.l: When the night came, he was a handsome man and the wedding was celebrated with splendour.
sentences.i: When night came he was a handsome man, and the wedding was held with great splendour.
sentences.n: schön of a man is handsome. Pracht is display, magnificence — the word returns whenever this tale holds a feast.

sentences.t: Sie lebten vergnügt mit einander, wachten in der Nacht und schliefen am Tag.
sentences.l: They lived contentedly with one another, were awake in the night and slept by day.
sentences.i: They lived happily together, waking by night and sleeping by day.
sentences.n: wachen is to be awake, not to watch over someone; the pair wachten … schliefen turns the ordinary day upside down, which is the whole point of the marriage.

sentences.t: Zu einer Zeit kam er und sagte „morgen ist ein Fest in deines Vaters Haus, weil deine älteste Schwester sich verheirathet,
sentences.l: At one time he came and said “tomorrow there is a feast in your father’s house, because your eldest sister is marrying,
sentences.i: One day he came and said, “Tomorrow there is a feast at your father’s house, for your eldest sister is being married,
sentences.n: Zu einer Zeit is the vague “at one time, one day.” deines Vaters Haus sets the genitive before its noun, an order English keeps in “your father’s house.” verheirathet is the 1857 spelling of verheiratet.

sentences.t: und wenn du Lust hast hinzugehen, so sollen dich meine Löwen hinführen.“
sentences.l: and if you have a mind to go there, then my lions shall lead you there.”
sentences.i: and if you have any wish to go, my lions shall take you there.”
sentences.n: Lust haben is “to have a mind to.” The hin- of hinzugehen and hinführen marks motion away toward the place spoken of.

sentences.t: Da sagte sie ja, sie möchte gern ihren Vater wiedersehen, fuhr hin und ward von den Löwen begleitet.
sentences.l: Then she said yes, she would gladly see her father again, drove there and was accompanied by the lions.
sentences.i: Then she said yes, she would dearly like to see her father again; and she drove there with the lions for escort.
sentences.n: möchte gern is the subjunctive of reported speech — her own wish, given back in her words. fuhr is of travelling by carriage, gieng of going on foot; the tales keep the two apart.

sentences.t: Da war große Freude, als sie ankam, denn sie hatten alle geglaubt sie wäre von dem Löwen zerrissen worden und schon lange nicht mehr am Leben.
sentences.l: There was great joy when she arrived, for they had all believed she had been torn to pieces by the lion and long since no more among the living.
sentences.i: There was great rejoicing when she came, for they had all believed the lion had torn her to pieces and that she had long since ceased to be alive.
sentences.n: wäre … zerrissen worden is the subjunctive of reported belief, marking what they thought rather than what was so. am Leben sein is “to be alive.”

sentences.t: Sie erzählte aber was sie für einen schönen Mann hätte und wie gut es ihr gienge,
sentences.l: But she told what a handsome husband she had and how well it was going for her,
sentences.i: But she told them what a handsome husband she had and how well she was faring,
sentences.n: was für ein is the fixed phrase “what kind of, what a”; the für is not “for” here. es geht mir gut is impersonal — literally “it goes well to me” — where English gives the person the subject. Mann is husband as well as man.

sentences.t: und blieb bei ihnen so lang die Hochzeit dauerte, dann fuhr sie wieder zurück in den Wald.
sentences.l: and stayed with them so long as the wedding lasted, then she drove back again into the wood.
sentences.i: and she stayed with them as long as the wedding lasted, and then drove back into the forest.
sentences.n: so lang is the older spelling of solange, “as long as.”

sentences.t: Wie die zweite Tochter heirathete und sie wieder zur Hochzeit eingeladen war, sprach sie zum Löwen „diesmal will ich nicht allein sein, du mußt mitgehen.“
sentences.l: When the second daughter married and she was invited to the wedding again, she said to the lion “this time I will not be alone, you must go with me.”
sentences.i: When the second daughter married and she was invited to the wedding again, she said to the lion, “This time I will not go alone; you must come with me.”
sentences.n: heirathete is the 1857 spelling of heiratete. mitgehen is separable, the mit carrying “along with me.” mußt is the 1857 spelling of musst.

sentences.t: Der Löwe aber sagte das wäre zu gefährlich für ihn,
sentences.l: But the lion said that would be too dangerous for him,
sentences.i: But the lion said it would be too dangerous for him,
sentences.n: wäre is the subjunctive that marks reported speech: German needs no further “he said,” the verb form alone shows these are his words.

sentences.t: denn wenn dort der Strahl eines brennenden Lichts ihn berührte, so würde er in eine Taube verwandelt, und müßte sieben Jahre lang mit den Tauben fliegen.
sentences.l: for if there the ray of a burning candle touched him, then he would be changed into a dove, and would have to fly seven years long with the doves.
sentences.i: for if the beam of a burning candle touched him there, he would be turned into a dove and would have to fly with the doves for seven years.
sentences.n: Licht is both light and candle; here the candles of a wedding procession. würde … verwandelt is a passive in the unreal mood, and müßte is the 1857 spelling of müsste.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sagte sie, „geh nur mit mir: ich will dich schon hüten und vor allem Licht bewahren.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” said she, “only go with me: I will surely guard you and keep you from all light.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” she said, “do come with me: I shall watch over you and keep you from every light.”
sentences.n: nur with an imperative turns it into urging, “do go.” schon is again the reassuring particle. bewahren vor names the thing guarded against, “keep from.”

sentences.t: Also zogen sie zusammen und nahmen auch ihr kleines Kind mit.
sentences.l: So they journeyed together and took their little child along too.
sentences.i: So they travelled together and took their little child with them as well.
sentences.n: Also is “so, accordingly,” a false friend for English “also.” mitnehmen is separable: nahmen … mit.

sentences.t: Sie ließ dort einen Saal mauern, so stark und dick daß kein Strahl durchdringen konnte,
sentences.l: She had a hall walled there, so strong and thick that no ray could get through,
sentences.i: She had a hall built there of stone, so strong and thick that no beam of light could get through,
sentences.n: mauern is to build in stone, from Mauer, a wall; ließ … mauern is once more lassen with an infinitive, “had it built.”

sentences.t: darin sollt er sitzen, wann die Hochzeitslichter angesteckt würden.
sentences.l: therein he should sit, when the wedding candles were lit.
sentences.i: he was to sit inside it when the wedding candles were lit.
sentences.n: sollt is the 1857 form of sollte. wann stands here where modern German writes wenn, “when.” anstecken is separable, to set alight: angesteckt würden, a passive in reported speech.

sentences.t: Die Thür aber war von frischem Holz gemacht, das sprang und bekam einen kleinen Ritz, den kein Mensch bemerkte.
sentences.l: But the door was made of fresh wood, which sprang and got a little crack that no person noticed.
sentences.i: But the door was made of green wood, which split and got a small crack that nobody noticed.
sentences.n: Thür is the 1857 spelling of Tür. frisch of timber means unseasoned, green. springen of wood is to split — the same verb the lark does in the title, in a wholly different sense.

sentences.t: Nun ward die Hochzeit mit Pracht gefeiert,
sentences.l: Now the wedding was celebrated with splendour,
sentences.n: The wording repeats, word for word, the line used of her own wedding above; the repetition sets the two feasts side by side.

sentences.t: wie aber der Zug aus der Kirche zurückkam mit den vielen Fackeln und Lichtern an dem Saal vorbei, da fiel ein haarbreiter Strahl auf den Königssohn,
sentences.l: but as the procession came back from the church with the many torches and candles past the hall, there fell a hair’s-breadth ray upon the king’s-son,
sentences.i: but as the procession came back from church past the hall with all its torches and candles, a ray no wider than a hair fell on the prince,
sentences.n: vorbei belongs with an dem Saal, “past the hall,” and stands off at the end in the German way. haarbreit, of a hair’s breadth, carries the whole disaster: the wall held, the door did not.

sentences.t: und wie dieser Strahl ihn berührt hatte, in dem Augenblick war er auch verwandelt,
sentences.l: and as this ray had touched him, in that moment he was changed too,
sentences.i: and the instant the ray touched him he was transformed,
sentences.n: auch here is not “also” but the confirming particle, “sure enough, at once.” in dem Augenblick, in that instant.

sentences.t: und als sie hineinkam und ihn suchte, sah sie ihn nicht, aber es saß da eine weiße Taube.
sentences.l: and when she came in and sought him, she did not see him, but there sat a white dove.
sentences.i: and when she came in and looked for him, she did not see him, but a white dove was sitting there.
sentences.n: es saß da uses the placeholder es of existence, which English matches with “there sat.” hineinkommen is separable, hinein marking motion inward.

sentences.t: Die Taube sprach zu ihr „sieben Jahr muß ich in die Welt fortfliegen:
sentences.l: The dove said to her “seven years must I fly away into the world:
sentences.i: The dove said to her, “For seven years I must fly out into the world:
sentences.n: sieben Jahr keeps the old uninflected plural after a numeral, where modern German writes Jahre. fortfliegen is separable, fort “away.”

sentences.t: alle sieben Schritte aber will ich einen rothen Blutstropfen und eine weiße Feder fallen lassen,
sentences.l: but every seven steps I will let a red drop of blood and a white feather fall,
sentences.i: but at every seventh step I will let fall a red drop of blood and a white feather,
sentences.n: alle sieben Schritte is “every seven steps.” rothen is the 1857 spelling of roten. fallen lassen is lassen with an infinitive again, “to let fall.”

sentences.t: die sollen dir den Weg zeigen, und wenn du der Spur folgst, kannst du mich erlösen.“
sentences.l: these shall show you the way, and if you follow the trail, you can redeem me.”
sentences.i: they shall show you the way, and if you follow the trail you can set me free.”
sentences.n: folgen takes the dative: der Spur folgst. erlösen is the tales’ word for breaking a spell — to release, to redeem — and it runs through the rest of this story.

sentences.t: Da flog die Taube zur Thür hinaus, und sie folgte ihr nach,
sentences.l: Then the dove flew out at the door, and she followed after her,
sentences.i: Then the dove flew out through the door, and she followed after it,
sentences.n: hinaus belongs with zur Thür: zur Thür hinaus, “out at the door.” nachfolgen is separable and takes the dative: folgte ihr nach. Taube is feminine in German, so the bird is “she” all through; English can only manage “it.”

sentences.t: und alle sieben Schritte fiel ein rothes Blutströpfchen und ein weißes Federchen herab und zeigte ihr den Weg.
sentences.l: and every seven steps a little red drop of blood and a little white feather fell down and showed her the way.
sentences.i: and at every seventh step a small red drop of blood and a small white feather fell and showed her the way.
sentences.n: Blutströpfchen and Federchen are diminutives of Blutstropfen and Feder — what the dove promised, now made small and pitiable. herabfallen is separable: fiel … herab.

sentences.t: So gieng sie immer zu in die weite Welt hinein, und schaute nicht um sich und ruhte sich nicht, und waren fast die sieben Jahre herum:
sentences.l: So she went ever on into the wide world, and looked not about her and rested not, and the seven years were nearly round:
sentences.i: So she went straight on into the wide world, never looking about her and never resting, and the seven years were almost up:
sentences.n: immer zu is the old “on and on.” sich umschauen and sich ausruhen are both reflexive. herum sein of a stretch of time is “to be up, to be over.”

sentences.t: da freute sie sich und meinte sie wären bald erlöst, und war noch so weit davon.
sentences.l: then she rejoiced and thought they were soon redeemed, and was still so far from it.
sentences.i: then she was glad and thought they would soon be free, and she was still so far from it.
sentences.n: wären is the subjunctive of her own thought, not of the fact. The closing clause und war noch so weit davon carries no subject at all in German; the flatness of it is the point.

sentences.t: Einmal, als sie so fortgieng, fiel kein Federchen mehr und auch kein rothes Blutströpfchen, und als sie die Augen aufschlug, so war die Taube verschwunden.
sentences.l: Once, as she was going on so, no little feather fell any more and no little red drop of blood either, and when she raised her eyes, the dove had vanished.
sentences.i: Once, as she went on like this, no more feathers fell, and no more red drops of blood either, and when she lifted her eyes the dove had vanished.
sentences.n: fortgieng is the 1857 spelling of fortging, from the separable fortgehen. die Augen aufschlagen is the set phrase for lifting one’s eyes.

sentences.t: Und weil sie dachte „Menschen können dir da nicht helfen,“
sentences.l: And because she thought “men cannot help you there,”
sentences.i: And because she thought, “No one on earth can help you here,”
sentences.n: She addresses herself as du in her own thoughts, which German does readily. Menschen with no article means people at large, human beings as against sun, moon and wind — which is where she turns next.

sentences.t: so stieg sie zur Sonne hinauf und sagte zu ihr „du scheinst in alle Ritzen und über alle Spitzen, hast du keine weiße Taube fliegen sehen?“
sentences.l: so she climbed up to the sun and said to her “you shine into all the cracks and over all the peaks, have you seen no white dove flying?”
sentences.i: so she climbed up to the sun and said to her, “You shine into every crack and over every peak — have you seen no white dove flying?”
sentences.n: die Sonne is feminine, so the sun is addressed as a woman; der Mond, coming next, is a man. Ritzen … Spitzen is a jingle, and the rhyme is part of the asking. fliegen sehen is the bare infinitive after a verb of perception.

sentences.t: „ Nein,“ sagte die Sonne, „ich habe keine gesehen, aber da schenk ich dir ein Kästchen, das mach auf, wenn du in großer Noth bist.“
sentences.l: “No,” said the sun, “I have seen none, but here I make you a present of a little box; open that when you are in great need.”
sentences.i: “No,” said the sun, “I have seen none; but here I give you a little casket — open it when you are in great need.”
sentences.n: The 1857 printing has a space after the opening quotation mark here, an accident of the setting, and it is left as it stands. schenk and mach drop the -e of the imperative, as speech does. Noth is the 1857 spelling of Not, need or distress.

sentences.t: Da dankte sie der Sonne und gieng weiter bis es Abend war, und der Mond schien,
sentences.l: Then she thanked the sun and went further until it was evening, and the moon shone,
sentences.i: Then she thanked the sun and went on until evening came, and the moon shone,
sentences.n: danken takes the dative: dankte der Sonne, dankte dem Mond.

sentences.t: da fragte sie ihn „du scheinst ja die ganze Nacht und durch alle Felder und Wälder, hast du keine weiße Taube fliegen sehen?“
sentences.l: then she asked him “you shine indeed the whole night and through all the fields and woods, have you seen no white dove flying?”
sentences.i: then she asked him, “You shine all night long and over every field and forest — have you seen no white dove flying?”
sentences.n: ja inside a sentence is the particle of what both parties know already, “you shine, after all.” Wälder is the plural of Wald.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ sagte der Mond, „ich habe keine gesehen, aber da schenk ich dir ein Ei, das zerbrich wenn du in großer Noth bist.“
sentences.l: “No,” said the moon, “I have seen none, but here I make you a present of an egg; break that when you are in great need.”
sentences.i: “No,” said the moon, “I have seen none; but here I give you an egg — break it when you are in great need.”
sentences.n: The three helpers answer in nearly the same words each time; the tale is counting them off, and the English keeps the sameness rather than varying it.

sentences.t: Da dankte sie dem Mond, und gieng weiter, bis der Nachtwind heran kam und sie anblies:
sentences.l: Then she thanked the moon, and went further, until the night wind came up and blew upon her:
sentences.i: Then she thanked the moon and went on, until the night wind came up and blew on her:
sentences.n: heran kam (modern herankam) and anblies are both separable; the an of anblasen means the blowing is aimed at her.

sentences.t: da sprach sie zu ihm „du wehst ja über alle Bäume und unter allen Blättern weg, hast du keine weiße Taube fliegen sehen?“
sentences.l: then she said to him “you blow indeed over all the trees and away under all the leaves, have you seen no white dove flying?”
sentences.i: then she said to him, “You blow over every tree and in under every leaf — have you seen no white dove flying?”
sentences.n: weg belongs with wehst: unter allen Blättern weg, blowing away under the leaves. Blättern is the dative plural of Blatt.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ sagte der Nachtwind, „ich habe keine gesehen, aber ich will die drei andern Winde fragen, die haben sie vielleicht gesehen.“
sentences.l: “No,” said the night wind, “I have seen none, but I will ask the three other winds, they have perhaps seen her.”
sentences.i: “No,” said the night wind, “I have seen none; but I will ask the three other winds — perhaps they have seen her.”
sentences.n: vielleicht stands inside the clause where English puts “perhaps” at the head of it.

sentences.t: Der Ostwind und der Westwind kamen und hatten nichts gesehen,
sentences.l: The east wind and the west wind came and had seen nothing,
sentences.i: The east wind and the west wind came, and they had seen nothing,
sentences.n: The four winds are treated as persons, each with his own quarter of the sky; only the south wind has been where the dove went.

sentences.t: der Südwind aber sprach „die weiße Taube habe ich gesehen, sie ist zum rothen Meer geflogen, da ist sie wieder ein Löwe geworden, denn die sieben Jahre sind herum,
sentences.l: but the south wind said “the white dove I have seen, she has flown to the Red Sea, there she has become a lion again, for the seven years are round,
sentences.i: but the south wind said, “The white dove I have seen; she has flown to the Red Sea, and there she has become a lion again, for the seven years are up,
sentences.n: die weiße Taube stands first as object — the German way of putting the point of an answer up front, which English can copy here. rothen is the 1857 spelling of roten.

sentences.t: und der Löwe steht dort im Kampf mit einem Lindwurm, der Lindwurm ist aber eine verzauberte Königstochter.“
sentences.l: and the lion stands there in combat with a dragon, but the dragon is an enchanted king’s-daughter.”
sentences.i: and the lion stands there fighting a dragon, and the dragon is an enchanted princess.”
sentences.n: Lindwurm is the old word for a serpent-dragon, wingless and coiling. Königstochter, king’s daughter, is the tales’ word for a princess.

sentences.t: Da sagte der Nachtwind zu ihr „ich will dir Rath geben, geh zum rothen Meer, am rechten Ufer da stehen große Ruthen, die zähle,
sentences.l: Then the night wind said to her “I will give you counsel: go to the Red Sea, on the right bank there stand great rods, count those,
sentences.i: Then the night wind said to her, “I will give you counsel: go to the Red Sea; on the right bank there stand great rods — count them,
sentences.n: Rath is the 1857 spelling of Rat, counsel. Ruthen (modern Ruten) are rods or switches; what exactly is growing at the water is not said, so “rods” is left standing rather than made into reeds. die zähle again puts the object first.

sentences.t: und die eilfte schneid dir ab, und schlag den Lindwurm damit, dann kann ihn der Löwe bezwingen, und beide bekommen auch ihren menschlichen Leib wieder.
sentences.l: and cut yourself off the eleventh, and strike the dragon with it, then the lion can overcome him, and both get their human body back again.
sentences.i: and cut off the eleventh for yourself, and strike the dragon with it; then the lion can overcome him, and both will have their human bodies again.
sentences.n: eilfte is the 1857 spelling of elfte. schneid dir ab has the dative of advantage, “cut for yourself,” and abschneiden is separable. Leib is the body as flesh, over against Gestalt, the shape a spell puts on.

sentences.t: Hernach schau dich um, und du wirst den Vogel Greif sehen, der am rothen Meer sitzt, schwing dich mit deinem Liebsten auf seinen Rücken:
sentences.l: Afterwards look about you, and you will see the bird Greif, which sits by the Red Sea; swing yourself with your dearest onto his back:
sentences.i: Afterwards look about you, and you will see the griffin that sits by the Red Sea; swing yourself onto his back with your beloved:
sentences.n: der Vogel Greif — the griffin, named as “the bird Greif,” the way one names a person. sich schwingen is reflexive, to swing oneself up. Liebster, used as a noun, is the tales’ word for the beloved.

sentences.t: der Vogel wird euch übers Meer nach Haus tragen.
sentences.l: the bird will carry you over the sea home.
sentences.i: the bird will carry you home across the sea.
sentences.n: euch is the plural “you,” now that there will be two of them. nach Haus (modern nach Hause) is the fixed phrase for homeward.

sentences.t: Da hast du auch eine Nuß, wenn du mitten über dem Meere bist, laß sie herab fallen,
sentences.l: There you have a nut too, when you are in the middle over the sea, let it fall down,
sentences.i: Here, take a nut as well; when you are halfway across the sea, let it drop,
sentences.n: Da hast du is the ordinary “here, take this.” Meere carries the old dative -e, now gone. herab fallen lassen is lassen with an infinitive once more.

sentences.t: alsbald wird sie aufgehen, und ein großer Nußbaum wird aus dem Wasser hervor wachsen, auf dem sich der Greif ausruht:
sentences.l: at once it will open, and a great nut tree will grow forth out of the water, on which the griffin rests himself:
sentences.i: at once it will open, and a great nut tree will grow up out of the water, and on it the griffin will rest:
sentences.n: aufgehen of a seed is to sprout, of a door to open, and the two senses lie close together here. hervor wachsen is written apart in 1857 where modern German writes hervorwachsen. sich ausruhen is reflexive.

sentences.t: und könnte er nicht ruhen, so wäre er nicht stark genug euch hinüber zu tragen:
sentences.l: and could he not rest, then he would not be strong enough to carry you over:
sentences.i: and if he could not rest, he would not be strong enough to carry you across:
sentences.n: The condition is made by putting the verb first, könnte er nicht ruhen, “if he could not rest”; both verbs stand in the subjunctive, since it is only supposed.

sentences.t: und wenn du vergißt die Nuß herab zu werfen, so läßt er euch ins Meer fallen.“
sentences.l: and if you forget to throw the nut down, then he lets you fall into the sea.”
sentences.i: and if you forget to throw the nut down, he will let you fall into the sea.”
sentences.n: vergißt is the 1857 spelling of vergisst. herab zu werfen is written in three words here, where modern German writes herabzuwerfen.

sentences.t: Da gieng sie hin und fand alles wie der Nachtwind gesagt hatte.
sentences.l: Then she went there and found everything as the night wind had said.
sentences.n: hingehen is separable, the hin marking motion toward the place spoken of: gieng … hin.

sentences.t: Sie zählte die Ruthen am Meer und schnitt die eilfte ab, damit schlug sie den Lindwurm, und der Löwe bezwang ihn:
sentences.l: She counted the rods by the sea and cut off the eleventh, with it she struck the dragon, and the lion overcame him:
sentences.i: She counted the rods at the sea and cut off the eleventh; with it she struck the dragon, and the lion overcame him:
sentences.n: damit, “with that,” is the compound German uses in place of “with it.” bezwang is the past of bezwingen, to subdue.

sentences.t: alsbald hatten beide ihren menschlichen Leib wieder.
sentences.l: at once both had their human body again.
sentences.i: and at once both of them had their human bodies again.
sentences.n: alsbald is the tales’ “straightway, at once.”

sentences.t: Aber wie die Königstochter, die vorher ein Lindwurm gewesen war, vom Zauber frei war,
sentences.l: But as the king’s-daughter, who had been a dragon before, was free of the spell,
sentences.i: But as soon as the princess, who had been a dragon before, was free of the spell,
sentences.n: wie again means “when, as soon as.” Zauber is the spell itself, the thing one is freed from.

sentences.t: nahm sie den Jüngling in den Arm, setzte sich auf den Vogel Greif, und führte ihn mit sich fort.
sentences.l: she took the youth in her arm, set herself on the bird Greif, and carried him away with her.
sentences.i: she took the young man in her arms, seated herself on the griffin, and carried him off with her.
sentences.n: in den Arm nehmen is singular in German where English says “in her arms.” fortführen is separable: führte … fort.

sentences.t: Da stand die arme weitgewanderte, und war wieder verlassen, und setzte sich nieder und weinte.
sentences.l: There stood the poor far-wandered one, and was forsaken again, and set herself down and wept.
sentences.i: There stood the poor far-travelled woman, forsaken once more, and she sat down and wept.
sentences.n: die weitgewanderte is an adjective used as a noun, printed small in the 1857 text; she is given no name in this tale, only what she has done. niedersetzen is separable and reflexive: setzte sich nieder, “set herself down.”

sentences.t: Endlich aber ermuthigte sie sich und sprach „ich will noch so weit gehen als der Wind weht und so lange als der Hahn kräht, bis ich ihn finde.“
sentences.l: But at last she took heart and said “I will go yet as far as the wind blows and as long as the cock crows, until I find him.”
sentences.i: But at last she took heart and said, “I will go as far as the wind blows and as long as the cock crows, until I find him.”
sentences.n: sich ermuthigen (modern sich ermutigen) is to put courage into oneself. so weit … als and so lange … als are the older forms of soweit wie and solange wie. The line is a set formula of endurance, and weht and kräht rhyme in the German, which English cannot keep without straining.

sentences.t: Und gieng fort, lange lange Wege, bis sie endlich zu dem Schloß kam, wo beide zusammen lebten:
sentences.l: And went away, long long roads, until at last she came to the castle where the two lived together:
sentences.i: And she went on, over long, long roads, until at last she came to the castle where the two of them were living together:
sentences.n: The sentence opens with the verb and no subject at all, as spoken narrative does; the literal keeps the gap rather than filling it. lange lange Wege is an accusative of extent, “over long, long ways.”

sentences.t: da hörte sie daß bald ein Fest wäre, wo sie Hochzeit mit einander machen wollten.
sentences.l: there she heard that there would soon be a feast, where they wanted to hold their wedding with one another.
sentences.i: there she heard that there would soon be a feast at which the two of them were to be married.
sentences.n: wäre and wollten are the subjunctives of what she was told, not of what is so. Hochzeit machen is the plain phrase for holding a wedding.

sentences.t: Sie sprach aber „Gott hilft mir noch,“ und öffnete das Kästchen, das ihr die Sonne gegeben hatte,
sentences.l: But she said “God still helps me,” and opened the little box that the sun had given her,
sentences.i: But she said, “God will help me yet,” and opened the little casket the sun had given her,
sentences.n: noch here is “yet, still to come”: nothing has helped her so far, and she says God will. helfen takes the dative, mir.

sentences.t: da lag ein Kleid darin, so glänzend wie die Sonne selber.
sentences.l: there lay a dress in it, as shining as the sun herself.
sentences.i: and there lay a dress inside it, as bright as the sun herself.
sentences.n: darin, “therein.” die Sonne is feminine, so selber is “herself” — the gift matches the giver.

sentences.t: Da nahm sie es heraus und zog es an und gieng hinauf in das Schloß, und alle Leute, und die Braut selber, sahen sie mit Verwunderung an;
sentences.l: Then she took it out and put it on and went up into the castle, and all the people, and the bride herself, looked at her with wonder;
sentences.i: Then she took it out and put it on and went up into the castle, and all the people, and the bride herself, gazed at her in wonder;
sentences.n: herausnehmen, anziehen and ansehen are all separable, and all three particles drop to the end of their clauses: nahm … heraus, zog … an, sahen … an.

sentences.t: und das Kleid gefiel der Braut so gut, daß sie dachte es könnte ihr Hochzeitskleid geben, und fragte ob es nicht feil wäre.
sentences.l: and the dress pleased the bride so well that she thought it could make her wedding dress, and asked whether it were not for sale.
sentences.i: and the dress so pleased the bride that she thought it would do for her wedding dress, and she asked whether it was for sale.
sentences.n: gefallen turns the English round: the dress pleases the bride, where English says the bride likes the dress, and the person stands in the dative. geben here is not “to give” but “to make, to yield,” as in das gibt einen guten Braten: es könnte ihr Hochzeitskleid geben, “it could make her wedding dress.” feil is the old word for “to be had for money,” surviving only in feilbieten.

sentences.t: „Nicht für Geld und Gut,“ antwortete sie, „aber für Fleisch und Blut.“
sentences.l: “Not for money and goods,” she answered, “but for flesh and blood.”
sentences.n: Geld und Gut and Fleisch und Blut are set pairs, and Gut rhymes with Blut. The rhyme cannot be kept in English without forcing it, so the pairs are given plainly.

sentences.t: Die Braut fragte was sie damit meinte.
sentences.l: The bride asked what she meant by that.
sentences.n: damit once more, “by that” — the pronoun swallowed into the preposition.

sentences.t: Da sagte sie „laßt mich eine Nacht in der Kammer schlafen, wo der Bräutigam schläft.“
sentences.l: Then she said “let me sleep one night in the chamber where the bridegroom sleeps.”
sentences.i: Then she said, “Let me sleep one night in the chamber where the bridegroom sleeps.”
sentences.n: laßt is the plural imperative: she addresses the bride as ihr, the polite form, which comes into English simply as “let.” Kammer is a sleeping room, not a hall.

sentences.t: Die Braut wollte nicht, und wollte doch gerne das Kleid haben,
sentences.l: The bride would not, and yet would gladly have the dress,
sentences.i: The bride was unwilling, and yet she badly wanted the dress,
sentences.n: wollen with no infinitive after it means “to be willing”; doch marks the pull the other way.

sentences.t: endlich willigte sie ein, aber der Kammerdiener mußte dem Königssohn einen Schlaftrunk geben.
sentences.l: at last she consented, but the valet had to give the king’s-son a sleeping draught.
sentences.i: at last she consented, but the valet had to give the prince a sleeping draught.
sentences.n: einwilligen is separable: willigte … ein. Schlaftrunk is a glued compound, sleep-drink, a draught given to make him sleep.

sentences.t: Als es nun Nacht war und der Jüngling schon schlief, ward sie in die Kammer geführt.
sentences.l: When it was night now and the youth already slept, she was led into the chamber.
sentences.i: Now when night came and the young man was already asleep, she was led into the chamber.
sentences.n: ward … geführt is the old passive with ward for wurde. German schlief covers English “was asleep.”

sentences.t: Da setzte sie sich ans Bett und sagte „ich bin dir nachgefolgt sieben Jahre, bin bei Sonne und Mond und bei den vier Winden gewesen,
sentences.l: Then she set herself by the bed and said “I have followed after you seven years, have been with sun and moon and with the four winds,
sentences.i: Then she sat down by the bed and said, “I have followed after you seven years; I have been to the sun and the moon and the four winds,
sentences.n: nachfolgen takes the dative, dir. The second clause drops its subject ich, as speech does when the speaker has not changed.

sentences.t: und habe nach dir gefragt, und habe dir geholfen gegen den Lindwurm, willst du mich denn ganz vergessen?“
sentences.l: and have asked after you, and have helped you against the dragon, will you then forget me altogether?”
sentences.i: and I have asked after you, and I have helped you against the dragon — will you forget me altogether?”
sentences.n: nach jemandem fragen is “to ask after someone.” helfen takes the dative, dir. denn in a question is the particle of appeal, nearer to “then, after all” than to “for.”

sentences.t: Der Königssohn aber schlief so hart, daß es ihm nur vorkam als rauschte der Wind draußen in den Tannenbäumen.
sentences.l: But the king’s-son slept so hard that it only seemed to him as if the wind rustled outside in the fir trees.
sentences.i: But the prince slept so heavily that it only seemed to him as though the wind were rustling outside in the fir trees.
sentences.n: hart schlafen is to sleep deeply. es kam ihm vor is impersonal, “it seemed to him,” from separable vorkommen. als rauschte is the subjunctive after als, “as if it rustled.”

sentences.t: Wie nun der Morgen anbrach, da ward sie wieder hinausgeführt und mußte das goldene Kleid hingeben.
sentences.l: When now the morning broke, she was led out again and had to give up the golden dress.
sentences.i: When morning broke she was led out again and had to give up the golden dress.
sentences.n: anbrechen of the day is to break, as in English. hingeben is separable, to hand over, give away.

sentences.t: Und als auch das nichts geholfen hatte, ward sie traurig, gieng hinaus auf eine Wiese, setzte sich da hin und weinte.
sentences.l: And when that too had helped nothing, she grew sad, went out onto a meadow, sat herself down there and wept.
sentences.i: And when that too had been of no help, she grew sad, went out into a meadow, sat down there and wept.
sentences.n: nichts helfen is “to be of no use.” ward is again the old wurde: ward sie traurig, she grew sad.

sentences.t: Und wie sie so saß, da fiel ihr das Ei noch ein, das ihr der Mond gegeben hatte:
sentences.l: And as she sat so, there came into her mind the egg as well, which the moon had given her:
sentences.i: And as she sat there she remembered the egg the moon had given her:
sentences.n: einfallen is separable and takes the dative of the person: fiel ihr … ein, literally “it fell in to her,” which is how German says a thing occurs to you.

sentences.t: sie schlug es auf, da kam eine Glucke heraus mit zwölf Küchlein ganz von Gold,
sentences.l: she broke it open, then out came a brooding hen with twelve chicks all of gold,
sentences.i: she broke it open, and out came a mother hen with twelve chicks, all of gold,
sentences.n: aufschlagen is separable, here of breaking an egg open. Küchlein is a diminutive, little chicks; ganz von Gold, made entirely of gold.

sentences.t: die liefen herum und piepten und krochen der Alten wieder unter die Flügel, so daß nichts schöneres auf der Welt zu sehen war.
sentences.l: these ran about and cheeped and crept under the old one’s wings again, so that nothing more beautiful was to be seen in the world.
sentences.i: they ran about and cheeped and crept back under the old hen’s wings, so that there was nothing lovelier to be seen in the world.
sentences.n: der Alten is a dative of possession — literally “crept to the old one under the wings” — where English uses a possessive. zu sehen war is the German way of saying “was to be seen.”

sentences.t: Da stand sie auf, trieb sie auf der Wiese vor sich her, so lange bis die Braut aus dem Fenster sah,
sentences.l: Then she stood up, drove them on the meadow before her, so long until the bride looked out of the window,
sentences.i: Then she got up and drove them along the meadow in front of her, until at last the bride looked out of the window,
sentences.n: vor sich her treiben is to drive something along in front of oneself. The sie of trieb sie is the chicks, not the woman; German lets the context decide, English has to say “them.”

sentences.t: und da gefielen ihr die kleinen Küchlein so gut, daß sie gleich herab kam und fragte ob sie nicht feil wären?
sentences.l: and the little chicks pleased her so well that she came down at once and asked whether they were not for sale?
sentences.i: and the little chicks so pleased her that she came down at once and asked whether they were for sale?
sentences.n: gefallen once more with the person in the dative, ihr. The 1857 text closes this reported question with a question mark where a modern editor would not; it stands as printed.

sentences.t: „Nicht für Geld und Gut, aber für Fleisch und Blut; laßt mich noch eine Nacht in der Kammer schlafen, wo der Bräutigam schläft.“
sentences.l: “Not for money and goods, but for flesh and blood; let me sleep one more night in the chamber where the bridegroom sleeps.”
sentences.i: “Not for money and goods, but for flesh and blood; let me sleep one night more in the chamber where the bridegroom sleeps.”
sentences.n: The bargain comes back word for word from the first time; the tale repeats it whole, and the English repeats it too rather than varying the wording.

sentences.t: Die Braut sagte „ja,“ und wollte sie betrügen wie am vorigen Abend.
sentences.l: The bride said “yes,” and meant to cheat her as on the previous evening.
sentences.i: The bride said yes, and meant to cheat her as she had the evening before.
sentences.n: wollte here is intention, “meant to,” rather than “wanted to.” betrügen is to deceive outright.

sentences.t: Als aber der Königssohn zu Bett gieng, fragte er seinen Kammerdiener was das Murmeln und Rauschen in der Nacht gewesen sei.
sentences.l: But when the king’s-son went to bed, he asked his valet what the murmuring and rustling in the night had been.
sentences.i: But when the prince went to bed he asked his valet what the murmuring and rustling in the night had been.
sentences.n: gewesen sei is the reported-speech subjunctive inside the indirect question. Murmeln and Rauschen are verbs used as nouns — what he half heard through the sleeping draught.

sentences.t: Da erzählte der Kammerdiener alles, daß er ihm einen Schlaftrunk hätte geben müssen, weil ein armes Mädchen heimlich in der Kammer geschlafen hätte,
sentences.l: Then the valet told everything, that he had had to give him a sleeping draught, because a poor girl had secretly slept in the chamber,
sentences.i: Then the valet told him everything: that he had had to give him a sleeping draught, because a poor girl had slept secretly in the chamber,
sentences.n: hätte … geben müssen and hätte … geschlafen are subjunctives of reported speech, the valet’s account given back in his own mouth. geben müssen is the double infinitive again.

sentences.t: und heute Nacht sollte er ihm wieder einen geben.
sentences.l: and tonight he should give him one again.
sentences.i: and that tonight he was to give him another.
sentences.n: einen stands in for einen Schlaftrunk, “one of them.” sollte reports the order laid on him rather than his own intention.

sentences.t: Sagte der Königssohn „gieß den Trank neben das Bett aus.“
sentences.l: Said the king’s-son “pour the draught out beside the bed.”
sentences.i: The prince said, “Pour the draught out beside the bed.”
sentences.n: The sentence begins with the bare verb, with no Da or Und in front of it — a quick narrative turn the tales like. ausgießen is separable: gieß … aus.

sentences.t: Zur Nacht wurde sie wieder hereingeführt, und als sie anfieng zu erzählen wie es ihr traurig ergangen wäre,
sentences.l: At night she was led in again, and when she began to tell how sadly it had gone with her,
sentences.i: At night she was led in again, and when she began to tell how sadly things had gone with her,
sentences.n: es ist mir ergangen is impersonal — “it has gone with me” — where English gives the person the subject. anfieng is the 1857 spelling of anfing.

sentences.t: da erkannte er gleich an der Stimme seine liebe Gemahlin, sprang auf und rief „jetzt bin ich erst recht erlöst, mir ist gewesen wie in einem Traum,
sentences.l: then he knew at once by the voice his dear wife, sprang up and cried “now I am truly redeemed, it has been with me as in a dream,
sentences.i: he knew his dear wife at once by her voice, sprang up and cried, “Now at last I am truly set free; it has been with me as if in a dream,
sentences.n: an etwas erkennen is to know someone by a mark or a sound. erst recht is “properly, truly now”: she was freed from the dove-shape, and he only now from forgetting. mir ist gewesen is impersonal again. Gemahlin is the elevated word for a wife.

sentences.t: denn die fremde Königstochter hatte mich bezaubert, daß ich dich vergessen mußte, aber Gott hat noch zu rechter Stunde die Bethörung von mir genommen.“
sentences.l: for the strange king’s-daughter had enchanted me, so that I had to forget you, but God has taken the infatuation from me still at the right hour.”
sentences.i: for the strange princess had put me under a spell, so that I could not help forgetting you; but God has taken the delusion from me in good time.”
sentences.n: fremd is “strange, foreign, not one’s own.” daß here gives the result, “so that.” Bethörung (modern Betörung) is the state of having one’s mind turned — infatuation or delusion; which of the two is meant here the text does not settle, and both are left standing.

sentences.t: Da giengen sie beide in der Nacht heimlich aus dem Schloß, denn sie fürchteten sich vor dem Vater der Königstochter, der ein Zauberer war,
sentences.l: Then they both went secretly out of the castle in the night, for they were afraid of the father of the king’s-daughter, who was a sorcerer,
sentences.i: Then the two of them went secretly out of the castle in the night, for they were afraid of the princess’s father, who was a sorcerer,
sentences.n: sich fürchten vor is reflexive and takes the dative: “to be afraid of.” The sorcerer father is never seen; he exists only as the reason for the flight.

sentences.t: und setzten sich auf den Vogel Greif, der trug sie über das rothe Meer, und als sie in der Mitte waren, ließ sie die Nuß fallen.
sentences.l: and set themselves on the bird Greif, he carried them over the Red Sea, and when they were in the middle, she let the nut fall.
sentences.i: and seated themselves on the griffin, who carried them over the Red Sea; and when they were halfway across, she let the nut fall.
sentences.n: der trug sie is the loose relative again, literally “he carried them,” which English turns into “who carried them.” The night wind’s instruction is carried out to the letter.

sentences.t: Alsbald wuchs ein großer Nußbaum, darauf ruhte sich der Vogel, und dann führte er sie nach Haus,
sentences.l: At once a great nut tree grew, on it the bird rested himself, and then he carried them home,
sentences.i: At once a great nut tree grew up; the bird rested on it, and then carried them home,
sentences.n: darauf, “on it,” points back to the tree. sich ruhen is reflexive here, where modern German uses ruhen alone or sich ausruhen.

sentences.t: wo sie ihr Kind fanden, das war groß und schön geworden, und sie lebten von nun an vergnügt bis an ihr Ende.
sentences.l: where they found their child, it had grown big and beautiful, and they lived contentedly from then on until their end.
sentences.i: where they found their child, who had grown tall and beautiful; and from that time on they lived happily to the end of their days.
sentences.n: das war groß … geworden is the loose relative once more, “which had grown.” bis an ihr Ende is the tales’ closing formula for a life lived out to the end.
